exams.title: Chapter Exam: Technology All Around Us

questions.question_text: Which of the following devices relies on a computer program (software) to function?

options.text: A digital microwave oven with preset timers

questions.explanation: A digital microwave uses an embedded microchip running software routines to read inputs, manage cook times, and control power.

questions.question_text: What is the primary difference between Hardware and Software?

options.text: Hardware is digital instructions; Software is physical components
Hardware is the physical, touchable parts of a computer; Software is the digital programs that instruct the hardware
Software can be touched; Hardware cannot

questions.explanation: Hardware refers to the physical components you can touch (CPU, RAM, screen, keyboard). Software refers to the digital programs and operating systems that tell the hardware what to do.

questions.question_text: In the Input → Process → Output cycle, which component is primarily responsible for the 'Process' phase?
questions.explanation: The CPU is the primary computational brain that handles processing calculations and logical instructions.

questions.question_text: In digital circuits, the 'ON' state represents the digit ____, and the 'OFF' state represents the digit ____.
questions.explanation: In binary logic, electricity flowing (ON) is represented by 1, and electricity stopped (OFF) is represented by 0.

questions.question_text: Why do programmers write code in high-level languages like Python instead of writing 0s and 1s directly?

options.text: Because high-level languages are slower than 0s and 1s
Because programming languages are close to human language and are translated automatically into binary
Because computers cannot actually understand binary
Because 0s and 1s are forbidden in modern software

questions.explanation: High-level languages allow humans to write readable, logical code, while compilers and interpreters translate that code into binary (0s and 1s) for the computer.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: What is a Program?

questions.question_text: What is the most accurate definition of a computer program?

options.text: A random collection of graphics and colors
A precise, ordered sequence of instructions guiding a computer to solve a task or achieve a goal
A metal wire placed inside the screen

questions.explanation: A computer program is a systematic, sequential set of instructions designed to direct a machine toward a specific outcome.

questions.question_text: In what order does a computer read and execute code instructions by default?

options.text: Line-by-line from top to bottom in strict sequence
All lines simultaneously at the same instant

questions.explanation: Computers execute instructions sequentially, starting from the first line down to the last line in order.

questions.question_text: In a video game: 'If player coins reach 100, award an extra life.' What programming concept is this?
questions.explanation: This is a conditional statement: when the condition (coins >= 100) becomes True, the reward is granted.

questions.question_text: Which scenario represents the best use of a loop with a stopping condition?

options.text: Continuing to prompt the user for their password until they enter the correct one
Displaying the title of a website

questions.explanation: The attempt repeats continuously in a loop and stops only when the condition (password is correct) is satisfied.

questions.question_text: Why are loops considered one of the most powerful tools in software development?

options.text: They make code much longer and harder to read
They eliminate repetitive manual code and automate huge workloads with speed and efficiency
They remove the need for a processor

questions.explanation: Loops eliminate redundant code and allow programmers to process thousands of items effortlessly.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: Algorithms — The Art of Problem Solving

questions.question_text: What are the three essential requirements of any valid algorithm?

options.text: It must be in English, contain pictures, and run on a phone
It must be Clear (unambiguous), Finite (has an end), and Effective (solves the problem)
It must contain at least 1,000 steps

questions.explanation: A proper algorithm must have unambiguous steps, terminate after a finite number of steps, and correctly solve the intended problem.

questions.question_text: In standard flowchart diagrams, what does the Diamond shape represent?

options.text: Start or end of the program
A decision point asking a question with Yes/No branches

questions.explanation: The diamond symbol represents a decision or condition where logic splits into two paths (True/Yes or False/No).

questions.question_text: Can a computer execute pseudocode directly?

options.text: Yes, because computers understand all human writing
No, pseudocode is written for humans to plan logic and must be converted to a real programming language to run
Yes, if written in capital letters
Yes, if it has no spelling errors

questions.explanation: Pseudocode is an informal design tool for human readers; machines require actual programming languages.

questions.question_text: Forgetting to close a parenthesis ) or quotation mark " is what type of error?
questions.explanation: Forgetting required symbols like parentheses or quotes violates the grammar rules of the language, causing a Syntax Error that prevents the program from running.

questions.question_text: What is the key difference between an algorithm and code?

options.text: An algorithm is the logical plan to solve a problem; code is that plan written in a specific programming language
An algorithm works only on laptops, while code works only on phones
There is no difference; they are 100% identical

questions.explanation: An algorithm is the abstract problem-solving strategy, while code is its practical implementation in Python, JavaScript, C++, etc.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: Speaking to Computers in Plain English?

questions.question_text: Which of the following is easiest for a beginner human to read and understand?
questions.explanation: Python was intentionally designed with clean, English-like syntax to maximize human readability.

questions.question_text: Which programming language is the global #1 choice for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Data Science?
questions.explanation: Python's massive ecosystem of AI libraries (like TensorFlow and PyTorch) makes it the worldwide standard for AI.

questions.question_text: If your Python code has a syntax mistake on Line 10, what will the Python interpreter do?

options.text: Execute Lines 1 through 9 successfully, then stop at Line 10 and display an error
Refuse to run Line 1 at all
Skip Line 10 silently and run Line 11

questions.explanation: Because an interpreter executes line-by-line, it runs preceding lines until it encounters the invalid instruction.

questions.question_text: In Python, what does a line starting with a hashtag (#) signify?

options.text: A secret command for the processor
A comment for human readers that the computer completely ignores
An order to delete all files

questions.explanation: The # symbol marks a comment: notes written by developers to explain code to teammates and themselves.

questions.question_text: What is the primary difference between a Compiler and an Interpreter?

options.text: A Compiler translates the entire program into machine code beforehand, while an Interpreter translates and executes line-by-line on the fly
Compilers only work on phones; Interpreters only work on laptops
Interpreters remove the need for electricity

questions.explanation: Compilers produce standalone machine executables in advance, while interpreters translate instructions dynamically during execution.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: The World of the Web

questions.question_text: The unique digital address assigned to every device connected to the internet is known as an:
questions.explanation: An IP (Internet Protocol) address acts as a unique digital street address routing data packets directly to your device.

questions.question_text: When you open a website in your browser, who is the Client and who is the Server?

options.text: The remote server is the Client; your browser is the Server
Your web browser is the Client requesting content; the remote host computer is the Server responding with files

questions.explanation: Your browser (Client) initiates an HTTP request, and the web host (Server) serves the response containing HTML, CSS, and JS files.

questions.question_text: A button reads 'Buy Now', is styled in vibrant green, and displays a popup 'Item Added!' when clicked. What handles each piece in order?

options.text: HTML creates the button → CSS styles it green → JavaScript handles the click popup
CSS creates the button → JavaScript styles it → HTML handles the click

questions.explanation: HTML supplies the button element, CSS applies the green styling, and JavaScript responds to the click event.

questions.question_text: What does the 'S' stand for in HTTPS (https://)?
questions.explanation: HTTPS stands for HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure, meaning data transmitted between client and server is encrypted.

questions.question_text: What three core file types does a server send to your browser to render a complete webpage?
questions.explanation: Webpages are built using HTML for content structure, CSS for visual styles, and JavaScript for interactivity.

questions.question_text: In which of the following technological domains does Python lead the entire industry?
questions.explanation: Python is the undisputed leader in AI and Data Science thanks to top libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow.

questions.question_text: What unique capability makes JavaScript completely different from every other programming language?

options.text: It only works on Mac computers
It is the only programming language natively built into and supported by all web browsers worldwide
It is free while all other languages cost money

questions.explanation: JavaScript is the sole scripting language supported natively by every web browser on Earth without plugins.

questions.question_text: Designing how video thumbnails appear on Instagram and styling the heart like button is the job of:
questions.explanation: Everything visual and interactive that users see and touch on screen is crafted by frontend developers.

questions.question_text: What title is given to a software engineer who can build both the Frontend and the Backend of an application?
questions.explanation: A Full-Stack Developer has the versatile skillset to build client-side interfaces and server-side logic.

questions.question_text: What is the best mindset when writing your first lines of real code?

options.text: Giving up whenever an error message appears
Reading error messages calmly, experimenting with hands-on practice, and knowing that every bug is a learning step

questions.explanation: Great programmers embrace challenges, learn from debugging, and build expertise through active practice.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: The Python Interpreter & Script Execution

questions.question_text: What happens when you run a Python script?

options.text: The computer translates the entire program into binary before running anything
The Python interpreter reads the program from top to bottom and executes each statement immediately
Python waits for all syntax errors to be fixed before starting
Only the last line of the script is executed

questions.explanation: Python is an interpreted language. The interpreter reads and executes the code line by line from top to bottom.

questions.question_text: What does the `end` parameter of the `print()` function control?

options.text: What is printed at the very end of the line (default is a newline)
How many times the text is printed

questions.explanation: By default `end='\n'`. You can change it (for example `end=' '`) to keep the next print on the same line.

questions.question_text: What does the Python interpreter do with everything written after the `#` symbol on a line?

options.text: It treats it as an error
It ignores it completely (it is a comment)
It prints it to the screen

questions.explanation: Single-line comments start with `#`. The interpreter ignores everything after the `#` on that line.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between a SyntaxError and a logical error?

options.text: A SyntaxError violates Python grammar so the code will not even start; a logical error runs but produces the wrong result
A logical error prevents the program from starting

questions.explanation: Syntax errors are caught during parsing before any line runs. Logical (or runtime) errors occur while the program is executing and produce incorrect results.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: Variables, Types & Memory Binding

questions.question_text: Does Python require you to declare the type of a variable before creating it?

options.text: Yes, you must always write the type first
No, Python is dynamically typed and determines the type from the assigned value

questions.explanation: Python is dynamically typed. It inspects the value you assign and automatically assigns the appropriate type.

questions.question_text: What happens when you reassign a variable in Python?

options.text: The old value is permanently deleted from memory
The variable name is rebound to a new value in memory
The type of the variable can never change

questions.explanation: Variables in Python are labels bound to objects in memory. Reassignment simply points the label to a different object.

questions.question_text: Which function converts the string `"12.5"` into a number that can be used in calculations?
questions.explanation: `float("12.5")` converts the string to a floating-point number so you can perform arithmetic with it.

questions.question_text: What is the modern and cleanest way to embed variables inside a string in Python 3.6+?
questions.explanation: f-strings (formatted string literals) allow you to write expressions directly inside curly braces after placing an `f` before the quotes.

questions.question_text: According to operator precedence (PEMDAS), what is the value of `10 + 2 * 5`?
questions.explanation: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so `2 * 5` is calculated first (10), then `10 + 10 = 20`.

questions.question_text: What does the modulo operator `%` return?

options.text: The integer quotient of a division
The floating-point result of a division

questions.explanation: `%` returns the remainder after division. For example, `14 % 4` equals 2.

questions.question_text: What is the short way to write `score = score + 10`?
questions.explanation: `+=` is the compound assignment operator. `score += 10` is equivalent to `score = score + 10`.

questions.question_text: What is the result of `28 % 5`?
questions.explanation: 5 goes into 28 five times (25), leaving a remainder of 3.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: Boolean Expressions & Conditional Branching

questions.question_text: Which operator checks if two values are NOT equal?
questions.explanation: `!=` is the “not equal” comparison operator in Python.

questions.question_text: What does the `and` logical operator require?

options.text: At least one operand must be True
Exactly one operand must be True

questions.explanation: `and` returns True only when both sides are True.

questions.question_text: In an `if-elif-else` ladder, what happens when the first condition is True?

options.text: Python still checks all remaining elif and else branches
Python executes that branch and skips all remaining elif and else branches

questions.explanation: As soon as one branch succeeds, Python executes its block and skips the rest of the ladder.

questions.question_text: What does the chained comparison `20 <= pressure <= 50` mean?
questions.explanation: Python allows mathematical chaining. `20 <= pressure <= 50` is shorthand for `pressure >= 20 and pressure <= 50`.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: Iteration & Sequences with for Loops

questions.question_text: How does Python’s `for` loop iterate over a list?

options.text: You must always use index numbers
It acts as a for-each loop and visits every element automatically

questions.explanation: Python’s `for` loop is a direct sequence iterator: `for item in items:` grabs each item one by one.

questions.question_text: What does `range(start, stop, step)` generate?

options.text: Numbers from start up to and including stop, stepping by step
Numbers from start up to (but not including) stop, stepping by step

questions.explanation: `range` stops before the stop value. Example: `range(0, 15, 5)` produces 0, 5, 10.

questions.question_text: What is the Accumulator Pattern?

options.text: A way to reverse a list
Initializing a total (or count) outside the loop and updating it inside the loop
A special type of for loop
A method that only works with dictionaries

questions.explanation: You create a running total or count variable before the loop and add to it on every iteration.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: Event-Driven & State-Based while Loops

questions.question_text: What is a sentinel value in a while loop?

options.text: A special signal value that tells the loop to stop
The first value printed by the loop

questions.explanation: A sentinel is a special value (like 0 or "quit") that causes the loop condition to become False and stop the loop.

questions.question_text: What is a common way to control a while loop using a boolean flag?

options.text: Set a flag to True before the loop and change it to False inside the loop when you want to stop
Flags only work with for loops
Flags are not allowed in Python

questions.explanation: A boolean flag (e.g., `is_running = True`) is checked in the while condition and set to False when the loop should end.

questions.question_text: What does the `break` statement do inside a loop?

options.text: Skips the current iteration and continues with the next one
Restarts the loop from the beginning

questions.explanation: `break` exits the loop immediately, regardless of the loop condition.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of an input validation loop?

options.text: To make the program run faster
To keep asking the user for input until the data is valid
To convert all input to strings
To skip invalid input without asking again

questions.explanation: Validation loops repeatedly prompt the user until the entered data meets the required constraints.

questions.question_text: What does negative indexing do with strings?

options.text: It counts backwards from the end of the string (-1 is the last character)

questions.explanation: `string[-1]` gives the last character, `string[-2]` the second-to-last, and so on.

questions.question_text: What does the slice `code[0:4]` return for `code = "TELEMETRY"`?
questions.explanation: Slicing `[start:stop]` extracts characters from start up to (but not including) stop. Indices 0-3 are T, E, L, E.

questions.question_text: What does the method `.upper()` do to a string?

options.text: It modifies the original string in place
It returns a new string with all characters converted to uppercase
It converts only the first letter

questions.explanation: Strings are immutable. Methods like `.upper()` return a new string; the original remains unchanged.

questions.question_text: What does `"X10:Y20".split(":")` return?
questions.explanation: `.split(sep)` divides the string at every occurrence of the separator and returns a list of the resulting pieces.

questions.question_text: Are lists mutable in Python?

options.text: No, lists cannot be changed after creation
Yes, you can change elements, add, and remove items after creation

questions.explanation: Lists are mutable. You can update items with index assignment, and use methods like append, insert, pop, and remove.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between `.append(x)` and `.insert(i, x)`?

options.text: append adds at the beginning; insert adds at the end
append always adds to the end; insert adds at a specific index
They do exactly the same thing

questions.explanation: `.append(x)` adds to the very end. `.insert(index, x)` injects the item at the given position.

questions.question_text: Which built-in function returns the largest value in a list of numbers?
questions.explanation: `max(list)` returns the maximum value. Related functions are `min()`, `sum()`, and `len()`.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between `list.sort()` and `sorted(list)`?

options.text: list.sort() modifies the original list in place; sorted(list) returns a new sorted list and leaves the original unchanged

questions.explanation: `.sort()` changes the list itself. `sorted()` creates and returns a brand-new sorted copy.

questions.question_text: How do you create a dictionary in Python?

options.text: Using curly braces {} with key: value pairs

questions.explanation: Dictionaries are written with curly braces and colon-separated key-value pairs: `{"name": "Alex", "age": 14}`.

questions.question_text: How do you add a new key-value pair to an existing dictionary?
questions.explanation: Assigning to a key either updates the value if the key exists or inserts a new key-value pair if it does not.

questions.question_text: Which method allows you to loop over both keys and values at the same time?
questions.explanation: `.items()` returns (key, value) pairs that you can unpack in a for loop: `for k, v in d.items():`.

questions.question_text: What is a common way to model a collection of records (like students or crew members)?
questions.explanation: A list containing dictionary objects is the standard way to represent tables, databases, and JSON-like data.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: Modular Functions & Reusable Logic

questions.question_text: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?

options.text: Parameters are the variable names in the function definition; arguments are the actual values passed when calling the function
Arguments are written in the def line; parameters are used when calling

questions.explanation: In `def compute_speed(distance, time):` the names distance and time are parameters. In `compute_speed(100, 2)` the values 100 and 2 are arguments.

questions.question_text: Why is it better for a function to return a value instead of just printing it?

options.text: Returning a value lets other parts of the program reuse, store, or calculate with that result
Printing is not allowed inside functions

questions.explanation: A pure function that returns a value is predictable, testable, and reusable. Printing is a side effect.

questions.question_text: What is the scope of a variable created inside a function?

options.text: Global – it can be seen everywhere
Local – it only exists while that function is running
It depends on the variable name
It becomes permanent after the first call

questions.explanation: Variables defined inside functions are local. They disappear when the function returns.

questions.question_text: What does the slice `"SPS Code Orbit"[4:8]` return?
questions.explanation: Indexing starts at 0. `[4:8]` takes characters at positions 4, 5, 6, 7 which are C, o, d, e.

questions.question_text: You run `result = "Hello".replace("l", "r")` then `print("Hello")`. What prints?

options.text: Nothing — the replace modified in place

questions.explanation: String methods never modify the original string because strings are immutable. `.replace()` returns a new string. We printed the original unchanged string.

questions.question_text: What does `f"{3.14159:.2f}"` produce?
questions.explanation: `:.2f` means format as a float with exactly 2 decimal places. Python rounds the result.

questions.question_text: A student writes `words = sentence.split()` then `print(len(words))`. What does this print?

options.text: The number of characters in the sentence
The number of words in the sentence

questions.explanation: `.split()` without arguments splits on spaces and returns a list of words. `len()` of that list gives the word count.

questions.question_text: What happens when you run `d = {"x": 1}` then `print(d["y"])`?
questions.explanation: Accessing a key that does not exist raises a KeyError. Use `.get()` to avoid the crash.

questions.question_text: `scores = {"Ali": 80}`. What does `scores.get("Sara", 0)` return?
questions.explanation: `.get("Sara", 0)` looks for the key. Because it does not exist, it returns the provided default value 0.

questions.question_text: What does `for key, value in my_dict.items():` do?

options.text: Loops through each key-value pair together

questions.explanation: `.items()` returns pairs like `("Ahmed", 95)`. Python unpacks each pair into `key` and `value`.

questions.question_text: In the grade book program, why is `grade_book.get(name)` better than `grade_book[name]` for the lookup function?

options.text: `.get()` returns `None` instead of crashing when the name does not exist

questions.explanation: If a student is not in the grade book, `dict[key]` raises KeyError. `.get()` safely returns None so you can print a friendly message.

questions.question_text: What is the main characteristic of a tuple?

options.text: It can be changed after creation

questions.explanation: A tuple is like a list with a lock — once created, its contents cannot be changed.

questions.question_text: How do you create a single-element tuple?
questions.explanation: A single-element tuple needs a trailing comma: `(42,)`. Without the comma it is just the integer 42.

questions.question_text: What is the main purpose of a set?

options.text: To store ordered data that can be changed

questions.explanation: Sets automatically keep only unique values and are useful for membership tests and removing duplicates.

questions.question_text: What is the output of `a, b = (5, 10)` then `a, b = b, a` then `print(a, b)`?
questions.explanation: First assignment gives a=5, b=10. Then `a, b = b, a` swaps them, resulting in a=10, b=5.

questions.question_text: Which mode opens a file for writing and creates it if it does not exist (overwriting existing content)?
questions.explanation: Mode "w" opens for writing. If the file exists it is truncated; if not it is created.

questions.question_text: What is the recommended way to open a file so that it is automatically closed?

options.text: Remember to call close() every time

questions.explanation: The `with` statement guarantees the file is closed even if an error occurs.

questions.question_text: Which module is commonly used for reading and writing CSV files?
questions.explanation: The built-in `csv` module provides reader and writer objects for working with comma-separated values.

questions.question_text: What does `os.path.exists(filename)` return?

options.text: True if the file or path exists, False otherwise
An error if the file does not exist

questions.explanation: It is a safe way to check whether a file exists before trying to open it.

questions.question_text: What will happen if you try to open a non-existent file in "r" mode without checking first?
questions.explanation: Reading a missing file raises FileNotFoundError. Always check existence or use try/except.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly imports only the `sqrt` function from the math module?
questions.explanation: `from module import name` brings a specific name into the current namespace.

questions.question_text: What does the `random` module provide?

options.text: Functions for generating random numbers and making random choices

questions.explanation: `random` is used for simulations, games, and any task that needs unpredictability.

questions.question_text: Which module is used to work with dates and times?
questions.explanation: The `datetime` module provides classes for manipulating dates and times.

questions.question_text: What does `import os` allow you to do?

options.text: Interact with the operating system (paths, files, environment)

questions.explanation: The `os` module gives access to operating-system functionality such as checking if a path exists.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between `import math` and `from math import pi`?

options.text: `import math` requires `math.pi`; `from math import pi` lets you use `pi` directly
`from math import pi` imports the whole module

questions.explanation: The first style keeps the module namespace; the second brings the name into the local namespace.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of a `try / except` block?

options.text: To catch and handle errors so the program does not crash

questions.explanation: Code that might fail is placed in the `try` block. If an exception occurs, the matching `except` block runs instead of crashing.

questions.question_text: What does the `finally` clause do?

options.text: It runs only when an error occurs
It always runs, whether an error occurred or not
It skips the rest of the code
It is required in every try block

questions.explanation: `finally` is useful for cleanup actions (closing files, releasing resources) that must happen in every case.

questions.question_text: What is a good practice when asking the user for a number?

options.text: Assume the user always types a valid number
Use a loop with try/except to keep asking until a valid number is entered

questions.explanation: Bulletproof input functions repeatedly prompt the user until the conversion succeeds.

questions.question_text: What keyword is used to deliberately raise an exception?
questions.explanation: `raise ValueError("message")` creates and raises an exception of the specified type.

questions.question_text:
What does the following list comprehension produce?

```python
[x*2 for x in range(5)]
```
questions.explanation: It multiplies every number from 0 to 4 by 2.

questions.question_text: How do you filter items inside a list comprehension?

options.text: Using an if clause at the end

questions.explanation: Example: `[x for x in numbers if x > 0]` keeps only positive numbers.

questions.question_text: What is a dictionary comprehension?

options.text: A way to create lists only
A concise way to build a dictionary from an iterable
A method that only works with sets

questions.explanation: Example: `{name: len(name) for name in names}` creates a dict mapping each name to its length.

questions.question_text:
What does the following produce?

```python
{x for x in [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]}
```
questions.explanation: A set comprehension automatically removes duplicates.

questions.question_text: What does a default argument look like in a function definition?
questions.explanation: You assign a default value with `=` in the parameter list.

questions.question_text: What do `*args` and `**kwargs` allow?

options.text: A variable number of positional and keyword arguments
They are used for returning values

questions.explanation: `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; `**kwargs` collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.

questions.question_text: What is a lambda function?

options.text: A small anonymous function defined with the `lambda` keyword
A function that can only return None

questions.explanation: Example: `square = lambda x: x * x`

questions.question_text: What is the scope rule for a variable created inside a function?

options.text: It is local to that function
It can be seen by all other functions automatically
Scope does not exist in Python

questions.explanation: Variables defined inside a function are local unless declared with the `global` keyword.

questions.question_text: Why must `self` always be the first parameter of every method in a class?

options.text: It is optional — Python works fine without it
Python automatically passes the object instance as the first argument when a method is called

questions.explanation: When you call `s.greet()`, Python translates it to `Student.greet(s)`. The method receives the object as `self`.

questions.question_text: What is the special method that runs automatically when you create a new object?
questions.explanation: `__init__` is the constructor. It is called when you write `Student("Ahmed", 10, 95)`.

questions.question_text: What does a method inside a class represent?

options.text: Behavior — what the object can do using its own data

questions.explanation: Methods are functions that belong to the class and can use `self` to access the object’s attributes.

questions.question_text: In the Classroom class, `self.students.append(Student(name, grade, score))` does what?

options.text: Creates a new Student object and adds it to the Classroom’s list of students
Adds a copy of the Classroom to the Student

questions.explanation: This is how one class manages a collection of objects of another class.

exams.title: Chapter Exam: Capstone — Building a Real Python Project

questions.question_text: Why is time spent planning before coding considered professional practice?

options.text: Companies require documentation for legal reasons
Planning reveals design problems early — when they are cheap to fix in comments, not expensive to fix in code
Clients want to see planning documents
Python requires a plan file before running

questions.explanation: Problems found in a plan take seconds to fix. Problems found after coding take hours to refactor.

questions.question_text: What Python data structure best represents a single student with a name, grade, and list of scores?

options.text: A class with name, grade, and scores attributes
A tuple — because it is immutable

questions.explanation: A class bundles data (attributes) and behavior (methods) together — the core idea of OOP.
